rwr.d: AWR's predecessor (Peters & Schaal, 2007): maximum likelihood on the policy's own actions, weighted by \(e^{\mathcal R/\beta}\), the exponential of the return. Without a baseline, high-return states dominate the gradient.

awac.d: Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (Nair, Gupta, Dalal & Levine): the same weight \(e^{A/\lambda}\) as AWR, with the advantage coming from a critic \(Q\); closed-form solution \(\pi^* \propto \pi_\beta\,e^{A/\lambda}\) without modeling the behavior policy. Uses \(\lambda = 0.3\) (manipulation) and 1.0 (MuJoCo).

a-lol.d: Advantage-based offline RL for language models (Baheti et al.): treats the whole response as a single action and trains only on the positive-advantage data, an AWR-style weighted SFT.

linha-de-base.d: A value that depends only on the state (or the prompt) and is subtracted from the reward: \(\mathcal R - b(s)\). It does not change the expected direction of the gradient, but it reduces variance and, in weighted-regression methods, evens out the scale of the weights between easy and hard states.

replay-buffer.d: A memory (usually FIFO) holding the most recent samples, reused across several training steps. The data becomes a mixture of past policies, which makes the method off-policy; in AWR, 50k samples with ~2,000 new ones per iteration.

corte-de-pesos.d: An upper limit \(\min(w, \omega_{\max})\) on the exponential weights of AWR and its relatives, which keeps a single sample from dominating the gradient when \(\beta\) is small. It trades a little bias for stability; the AWR paper uses \(\omega_{\max} = 20\).

bandit-contextual.d: A one-step decision problem: you see a context (the prompt), choose an action (the whole response) and receive a reward. It is the “per-sequence” reading of RLHF, in which there is no per-token credit.

raft.d: Dong et al.: generate \(K\) responses per prompt, keep the one with the highest reward and fine-tune on it, in rounds. It is the \(\beta \to 0\) limit of weighted SFT; the experiments use \(K \in \{8, 16, 32\}\).

rest.d: Gulcehre et al.: alternates Grow (the policy generates a dataset) and Improve (filter by increasing reward thresholds and fine-tune, each policy starting from the previous one with a smaller LR). The behavior cloning loss (NLL) was the best one in Improve.

rest-em.d: Singh et al. (“Beyond Human Data”): the generate → filter → fit loop read as EM, with a binary reward on MATH and APPS. The E-step builds \(q \propto p(O{=}1\mid x,y)\,\pi_{\theta_t}\); the M-step is a weighted NLL.

expert-iteration.d: Generic name for the loop sample → keep the good ones (verifier, judge) → do SFT on them → repeat with the new model. RFT, STaR, ReST-EM and Llama 2's rejection sampling are variations of it.

tamanho-efetivo-amostra.d: \((\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\): how many “real” samples sustain a weighted average. It equals \(K\) with equal weights and 1 when a single weight dominates; useful for checking whether a weighted SFT is resting on just a few examples.

infonce.d: The contrastive loss from CPC (van den Oord, Li & Vinyals, 2018): the cross-entropy of finding the positive among \(N\) candidates, \(-\log\big(f(x^+,c)/\sum_j f(x_j,c)\big)\). The optimum is the density ratio \(p(x\mid c)/p(x)\), and \(I \ge \log N - \mathcal L_N\). With 1 negative and the score \(\beta\log\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}}\), it is the DPO loss.

informacao-mutua.d: \(I(X;Y) = \mathbb D_{\text{KL}}\big(p(x,y)\,\|\,p(x)p(y)\big)\): how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other, in nats. InfoNCE gives a lower bound on it.

negativo-dificil.d: A negative example that the model still confuses with the positive (high score). In InfoNCE, each negative is pushed down with a strength equal to its softmax probability, so the hard ones receive almost all of the gradient.

slic.d: Sequence Likelihood Calibration (Zhao et al., 2022 and 2023): calibrates sequence log-probs with a hinge loss \(\max(0, \delta - \log P(y^+) + \log P(y^-))\) plus cross-entropy on the target as an anchor. SLiC-HF uses human preferences, margin 1.0 and LR \(10^{-5}\) on T5.

perda-hinge.d: \(\max(0, \text{margin} - m)\): zero once the margin \(m\) between positive and negative has passed the target, linear before that. Unlike the logistic loss, it zeroes out the gradient for pairs that are already solved. In TRL, loss_type="hinge" uses \(\max(0, 1 - \beta\Delta h)\).

cpl.d: Hejna et al. (ICLR 2024): models preferences between segments by regret (optimal advantage) and uses the maximum-entropy bijection \(A^* = \alpha\log\pi^*\) to obtain a supervised contrastive loss, convex and off-policy, without learning a reward or running RL. DPO is a special case.

arrependimento.d: How far a stretch of behavior falls short of the optimum, measured by the sum of the optimal advantages \(A^*\) along the stretch. CPL assumes that humans prefer by lowest regret, not by highest sum of rewards.

rl-maxima-entropia.d: RL that maximizes reward plus \(\alpha\) times the policy's entropy. The optimal policy is \(\pi^*(a\mid s) = e^{A^*(s,a)/\alpha}\), a bijection between advantage and policy. It is equivalent to KL regularization against the uniform policy.

unlikelihood.d: Welleck et al. (2019): adds \(-\alpha\sum_c\log(1 - p_\theta(c))\) to the cross-entropy, pushing down forbidden candidates (tokens from the previous context, repeated n-grams in decoded continuations). It fights repetition and overly frequent tokens.

awr-algoritmo.d: The details of the paper by Peng, Kumar, Zhang & Levine (2019): each iteration fits a critic \(V(s)\) by squared error (TD(λ) targets, λ = 0.95) and then the policy by maximum likelihood with weight \(\min(e^{(\mathcal R - V)/\beta}, \omega_{\max})\), with \(\beta = 0.05\) fixed, \(\omega_{\max} = 20\), a 50k-sample buffer and ~2,000 new samples per iteration.

kl-best-of-n.d: The classic formula \(\mathbb D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\text{bon}}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) = \log n - (n-1)/n\) (0.64 nat with \(n = 4\); 5.91 with 1,000) is an upper bound (Beirami et al., 2024): nearly exact when the \(n\) responses are distinct and there are no reward ties, loose with a binary reward or few possible responses. With a binary verifier and random tie-breaking, the KL never exceeds \(-\log P(\text{correct})\).

esperanca-maximizacao.d: An algorithm for maximizing a log of a sum (a likelihood with hidden variables) by climbing, coordinate-wise, a lower bound given by Jensen's inequality. The E-step picks the posterior distribution \(q\) (the bound becomes tight); the M-step maximizes \(\mathbb E_q[\log\pi_\theta]\), a weighted maximum likelihood. It is where the weights in RWR and ReST-EM come from.

nce.d: Gutmann & Hyvärinen (2010): estimate an unnormalized model by training a classifier to tell real data apart from samples of a known “noise” distribution. The normalization constant becomes one more parameter or drops out. InfoNCE is the version with one positive against \(N-1\) negatives.

ruidoso-racional.d: A model of human choice in which the better option is chosen more often, but not always: the probability of each option is a softmax of its quality (reward, or minus the regret). Bradley–Terry is the two-option case.
